author: County News Review
title: Flight 707 lifts Braham schools to new heights - NewsBreak
text:
13 hours ago
When the Braham Area Schools created their Flight 707 program three years ago, there was some push-back.
“People definitely were not embracing it [right away],” Superintendent Ken Gagner admitted. “There were a couple things at work. One was the impact on parents: Because their kids’ school day starts at 8, now it’s going to be starting at 9, that was the No. 1 concern.
“From the staff point of view, staff wanted to know what we were going to be doing. If our boss said, ‘I’m going to meet with you every single Monday, first thing in the morning,’ that would be a concern for any of us, right?”
What’s more, the school board was far from unanimous in its support, voting in favor of starting the program by a narrow 4-3 margin.
But three years later, the results of Flight 707 are becoming clear.
“I’m in year 40 of [working in] education, and from a leadership point, I think it’s the best thing I’ve done in my career,” Gagner said. “It’s not about brand. It’s a process that, to me, sets you up for success. …
“Every week we start off by getting together with our people and having a plan for the week. That’s how we’re going to be successful. … We have a clear plan in place every single week to meet the needs of our kids.”
Flight 707 is a program where teachers, staff and principals meet at 7:07 a.m. each Monday to discuss curriculum, teaching goals and issues, and a variety of other topics related to the effective teaching. To accommodate a 90-minute work session, the start of the school day on Monday is pushed back one hour, to 9 a.m.
Gagner explained that most schools have in-service days roughly once a month to address issues. Flight 707 meets every week, allowing for discussions and adjustments that can increase the chances for success.
Gagner said Flight 707 also helps create better teachers through collaboration with colleagues.
“If you look at all your workers, probably not every single one of them is a grade A,” he said. “When you put people together, you’re naturally going to learn from those who probably know the ropes a little bit. ...
“If a teacher is surrounded by the high fliers, plus they are held accountable each week, they will improve. Instead of shooting from the hip with a lesson plan, which isn’t going to fly, they have a plan for their week.”
Another reason Flight 707 has taken wing is that it has produced measurable results. In 2023 Braham’s graduation rate was 79.6%, which was 3.7% below the state average. For 2025 the number rose to 93.8% — the best percentage in this area, and 8.9% better than the state average.
“In every business you’ve got to have some measure of success, and [in education] we’ve got our measures,” Gagner said. “I like these measures because they’re not fluff — they show how we’re doing from an academic perspective. …
“Now that we’ve moved the bar way up, we’ve got to keep it up. It’s a lot easier to be at the bottom and work to improve than when you’re sitting in a better position, to keep that position and get better.
“Our focus now is to continue to improve. Don’t be satisfied, keep pushing the bar. We want to make sure now we keep moving the bar forward.”
Besides the demonstrable success, Gagner said there has been less push-back from parents and teachers because Flight 707 has become predictable.
“I really think our parents have adjusted,” he said. “They know that, if we don’t have school Monday, Flight 707 doesn’t move to Tuesday. It is only Mondays.
“I think our community has adapted. They know the routine. This is how things are on Mondays. I can’t honestly remember the last time someone mentioned something about Monday mornings.”
Gagner feels teachers also have warmed to the program as a way to continue improving.
“Now that our teachers know we’re not out to get them or anything, they realize that this is just a good way to start your week,” he said. “Whatever needs arise, we can jump on them. We don’t have to wait for two months for the staff development day. We can hit them every single Monday.
“If something comes up, we can address those things.”
Gagner said Flight 707 also helps address issues students may have, particularly at the upper levels.
“In high school a teacher sees a kid one hour, versus the elementary, where you have your kids all day,” he said. “It’s good to hear if little Johnny is struggling in the sixth hour, the first-hour teacher says, ‘Oh, I didn’t realize that’s an issue.’ And we can better meet those needs across the board.”
Another reason Gagner supports Flight 707 is that it did not cut down instruction time.
“I got the idea when I went to a conference, and I heard about where a school took a half day [for the program],” he said. “Schools had kids getting out an hour early or starting two hours late, and that took instruction away.
“We didn’t take a minute of instruction. We took two days that the kids had off. … If you shorten the amount of time you spend with kids to implement this, what are you doing? Our whole point is to be with kids.”
Gagner said he is especially proud of the way Flight 707 helps paraprofessionals succeed in their work with students who need support with instruction, behavior or personal care.
“Usually a paraprofessional in a school district shows up when the kids do, maybe 15 minutes before, and starts with kids when they get off the bus,” he said. “Here, our paras get a whole hour that they never had before. So every week, they get an hour to come in and get their week ready.
“And I just think they appreciate being valued.”
Flight 707 has started to garner attention in education circles around the state.
“We presented down at the Minnesota School Board Association at the leadership conference, which is held every January,” Gagner said. “I’ve shared it with colleagues in the Superintendent’s Association.
“Everybody likes the idea. I don’t know if they’re willing to do the lift, though, because it is a lot of work.”
Gagner said he welcomes calls from other schools to talk about bringing Flight 707 to their districts because it can be a win-win for everyone in the system.
“I think if I’m a teacher who’s showing up, and has a chance to work with their principals — why wouldn’t you want to work with your boss to be the best ever?” he said. “Why wouldn’t you want to work with your colleagues to be the best ever?
“In the elementary school, it’s more geared to visiting with your third grade partners, because everybody in third grade is teaching the same thing. In a high school, I’m the only one teaching choir or chemistry. But we still have things we can work on. … Alignment is what we’re working on right now. If the chemistry teacher changes a little bit, it does impact everybody else teaching science after that. And whatever is going on before you get your kids in chemistry impacts you in chemistry. So that’s where we need to be talking and communicating.”
Now Gagner says that fighting through that early push-back regarding Flight 707 was worth it.
“My favorite saying is, ‘doing what is right isn’t always easy, but it’s always right’,” he said. “Even though most people might feel I’m kind of overworked, I just need time, these meetings are about working with colleagues on a regular basis, having clear plans.
“And that does pay off. You might not see it instantly, but it does pay off. And now we’re seeing that. The success has been there.”
summary: If our boss said, ‘I’m going to meet with you every single Monday, first thing in the morning,’ that would be a concern for any of us, right?” What’s more, the school board was far from unanimous in its support, voting in favor of starting the program by a narrow 4-3 margin. We want to make sure now we keep moving the bar forward.” Besides the demonstrable success, Gagner said there has been less push-back from parents and teachers because Flight 707 has become predictable.
